entities.summary:
The Battle of Marathon was a pivotal battle fought on September 12, 490 BCE, between the city-state of Athens and the Persian Empire. This turning point in the Greco-Persian Wars showcased the bravery and strategic prowess of the Athenians, who defeated the Persians despite being outnumbered.

The battle took place on the plains of Marathon, a small town in ancient Attica, Greece. The Persian army, led by Datis and Artaphernes, had been marching through Greece, leaving destruction in their wake. The Athenians, led by the statesman Miltiades, devised a clever plan to defeat the Persians, using their knowledge of the terrain to their advantage.

The Athenians emerged victorious, inflicting heavy casualties on the Persian army. The battle marked a significant turning point in the Greco-Persian Wars, as it halted the Persian advance and boosted Athenian morale. The victory also solidified Athens' position as a major power in ancient Greece.

One of the lasting legacies of the Battle of Marathon is the famous phrase 'Come running, if you will,' attributed to the Athenian commander Miltiades. However, some historians argue that this phrase might be apocryphal, and its true origins remain unclear.

The Battle of Marathon had far-reaching consequences, shaping the course of Western history. It influenced the development of democracy in Athens and the spread of Greek culture throughout the Mediterranean. The battle also set a precedent for future conflicts between city-states and empires, demonstrating the power of strategic thinking and effective leadership.
